CPESR Exam 1 — Tagging Pilot

First 8 of 55 questions, transcribed + tagged from the image-based source. Format matches fs_simulator.html's schema (cat/topic/program).

Q1. Which among the following is/are true regarding LiDAR?
1. LiDAR is a surveying method that measures distance of a target by illuminating that target with a pulsed laser light, and measuring the reflected pulses with a sensor.
2. It is the most accurate data transmission technique in which light is used as medium.
IIlidar
  • A) 1 only
  • B) Neither 1 nor 2
  • C) 2 only
  • D) Both 1 and 2
LiDAR stands for Light Detection and Ranging, is a remote sensing method that uses light in the form of a pulsed laser to measure ranges (variable distances) to the Earth. These light pulses — combined with other data recorded by the airborne system — generate precise, three dimensional information about the shape of the Earth and its surface characteristics. LiDAR is a remote sensing technology that measures distance by illuminating a target with a laser and analyzing the reflected light. A LiDAR instrument principally consists of a laser, a scanner, and a specialized GPS receiver. LiDAR is highly accurate scientific surface/topographic data with active sensing system and it uses its own energy source, not reflecting naturally or naturally emitted radiation. This mode allows direct acquisition of terrain information.

Answer: A
Q2. A sewer lateral is to be installed at sta 21+37.45 on center. The connection to the sewer main (sewer wye) is 18 in in length. There is a break of the sewer line at sta 21+38.49. The break has to be cleared by a minimum of 6 in. The sewer main line must be inserted 3 in into the wye or any connecting pipe to secure it on both sides. What is the minimum distance that needs to be cut out of the sewer mainline to install the sewer wye and lateral?
Vconstr

  • A) 1.54 ft
  • B) 1.29 ft
  • C) 1 ft
  • D) 1.71 ft
First cut: 2138.49+0.5=2138.99 2138.99−18 in+3 in+3 in=2137.99 Second cut constrained at south end: 2137.45−5/12+3/12: second cut constrained at south end: 2137.45−\(\dfrac{5}{12}\)+\(\dfrac{3}{12}\)=2137.28 2138.99−2137.28=1.71 ft.

Answer: D
Q3. The field notes for a road centerline are shown (BM1 elev 111.73 through BM2 elev 110.67, with BS/FS readings and a 6+00 cross-section note). What is the slope from the centerline at Sta 4+00 to Sta 6+00, 60 ft right of centerline?
IIIlevel

  • A) 0.66%
  • B) −1.14%
  • C) 1.19%
  • D) −1.19%
Elev at 4+00 = 111.73+4.30−4.48 = 111.55 Length from Sta 4+00 to 60 ft right of Sta 6+00: Elev at 60 ft right of 6+00: elev at 60 ft right of 6+00 = 111.73+4.3−4.48+3.87−4.12+5.27−7.4 = 109.17 horizontal length = √(200²+60²) = 208.806 slope =\(\dfrac{(109.17-111.55)}{208.806}\)= −1.14%.
Note: The 3.7 in the notes is the FS for the centerline at sta 6+00. The numbers below the denominator are lengths from the centerline.

Answer: B
Q4. A new highway alignment requires a horizontal curve. Point A (N20324.77, E13965.48) is on the alignment before the curve; Point C (N20108.44, E19700.25) is after the curve; Point B (N22146.51, E16400.48) is the PI. What is the central angle of this curve?
IIItrav
  • A) 53°11'53"
  • B) 68°30'11"
  • C) 58°17'56"
  • D) 111°29'49"
Calculate latitude and departure for line AB, then find the bearing of AB: Latitude AB = 22146.51−20324.77 = 1821.74 Departure AB = 16400.48−13965.48 = 2435 Bearing AB = \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\text{Departure }AB}{\text{Latitude }AB}\right)\) Bearing AB = \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2435}{1821.74}\right)\)= 53.19808° = N53.19808°E Calculate latitude and departure for line BC, then find the bearing of BC: Latitude BC = 20108.44−22146.51 = −2038.07 Departure BC = 19700.25−16400.48 = 3299.77 Bearing BC = \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\text{Departure }BC}{\text{Latitude }BC}\right)\) Bearing BC = \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3299.77}{-2038.07}\right)\)= 58.29886° = S58.29886°E Use the given bearings to find the central angle: 180°−53.19808°−58.29886° = 68.5031° = 68°30'11"
Note: it is always best to draw a quick cross hairs with the bearings to make sure you are calculating the correct angle. Also keep degrees in decimal form until the end of the question to save time.

Answer: B
Q5. The survey crew is being asked to extend a level circuit across a canyon 1150 ft wide, with equipment access only from either side of the cliffs. Which technique should be used?
IIlevel
  • A) Spherical leveling
  • B) Cross sectional leveling
  • C) Reciprocal leveling
  • D) Concentrical leveling
Reciprocal leveling is utilized to extend a leveling circuit across a wide canyon, or other open barrier, by establishing a turning point of each side of the canyon from one side and taking a backsight on each to determine the height of instrument on the other side. By using the mean of the two HI determinations, the effects of curvature and refraction on the long sights are compensated.

Answer: C
Q6. A measurement was obtained using a steel tape found to be shorter than its actual length when the temperature was above standardized temperature. The temperature was consistent throughout the survey. What type of error is this?
IIItheory
  • A) Random error
  • B) Natural error
  • C) Cumulative error
  • D) Accidental error
A consistent temperature means the same error was applied to every measurement — a cumulative (systematic) error.

Answer: C
Q7. A surveying plane's flight height is 4,000 ft above sea level, camera focal length 8.25 in. What is the photo scale at Point 1 (elev 900 ft) and Point 3 (elev 125 ft)?
IVphoto

  • A) 1:566 / 1:479
  • B) 1:376 / 1:470
  • C) 1:576 / 1:870
  • D) 1:286 / 1:323
The scale of Points 1 and 3 are determined as follows: Scale = \(\dfrac{f}{(H-h)}\) Scale Point 1 = \(\dfrac{8.25\text{ in}}{(4{,}000\text{ ft}-900\text{ ft})}\) = 1 in = 375.76 Scale Point 3 = \(\dfrac{8.25\text{ in}}{(4{,}000\text{ ft}-125\text{ ft})}\) = 1 in = 469.69
Note: The easy way to determine the scale starting with 1 in is to divide the denominator by numerator. For example for point 1, it would be 3100/8.25=375.76. So the scale would be 1 in=375.76 ft.

Answer: B
Q8. The area of Lot ABC: CB = N82°15'E, 486.99 ft; CA = S40°00'E, 432.12 ft. What is the area?
IIItravProgram T — full

  • A) 1.97 ac
  • B) 2.04 ac
  • C) 1.88 ac
  • D) 2.13 ac
Angle C = 180−82°15'−40°00' = 57°45' A = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(CA)(CB)\sin C \times \dfrac{1\text{ ac}}{43{,}560\text{ ft}^2}\)= 2.04 ac

Answer: B
Q9. The grade of the centerline of a highway section from sta 7+22 to sta 11+35, elevations 147.23 ft and 163.77 ft respectively, is
Vvc
  • A) 3.60%
  • B) 3.80%
  • C) 4.00%
  • D) −4.00%
Grade =\(\dfrac{ΔElev}{ΔStation}\)=\(\dfrac{(163.77-147.23)}{(1135-722)}\)= 4%.

Answer: C
Q10. The radius of the circular curve is 641.13' and I=117°51'. If the forward tangent is offset 48 ft out, the radius needed to hold BC at the same location is
VhcProgram S — partial

  • A) 681.36 ft
  • B) 673.85 ft
  • C) 637.56 ft
  • D) 789.46 ft
T = R·tan(\(\dfrac{I}{2}\)) = 1063.86 ft The offset triangle's angle at EC is 180°−I = 62°9'. Offset x-component via this triangle: offset x-component = \(\dfrac{48}{\sin(62°9')}\)= 54.29 ft T' = T + offset x-component = 1063.86+54.29 = 1118.15 ft solve R' =\(\dfrac{T'}{\tan(I/2)}\)= 673.85 ft

Answer: B
Q11. A redesigned highway has shoulder-to-shoulder width 44 ft; a curve must clear a light pole by 9 ft on the outside edge (pole is 17 ft off centerline, I=24°53'40"). What is the centerline radius?
Vhc

  • A) 1994.12 ft
  • B) 2492.64 ft
  • C) 2042.12 ft
  • D) 1080.25 ft
E for centerline: 17 ft + 9 ft clearance + 22 ft to centerline of highway = E for centerline E = 48 ft E = \(R\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\dfrac{I}{2}}-1\right)\) 48 = \(R\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\dfrac{24°53'40''}{2}}-1\right)\) R = 1994.12 ft
Note: You might be tempted to find the E for the outside edge of the highway then find the radius of the outside edge of the highway. From there you may have subtracted 22 feet to get the radius of the centerline. This approach is wrong because doing so would change the tangent points and lengths and would also change the "I". In this situation, we must hold those fixed since we are provided the I value and the problem stated that the highway is fixed.

Answer: A
Q12. BVC sta 5+00 elev 250.00, +5.5% grade in; EVC sta 29+00 elev 358.00, +3.5% grade out. Typical cross section: 22 ft to edge at 2%, then 10 ft at 2% down to toe, 6" curb. What is the elevation of the toe of slope at sta 19+50?
VvcProgram P — partial

  • A) 320.79 ft
  • B) 321.03 ft
  • C) 320.89 ft
  • D) 321.25 ft
19+50 − 5+00 = 1450 ft \(\text{elev}_{19-50}=\dfrac{Rx^{2}}{2}+g_1x+\text{elev}_{BVC}\) \(R=\dfrac{g_2-g_1}{L}=\dfrac{3.5-5.5}{24}\)= −0.08333 elev at 19+50 = −0.08333(14.5)²/2 + 5.5(14.5) + 250 elev at 19+50 = 320.99 ft toe = 320.99 − (22×0.02) + 0.5 + (10×0.02) toe = 321.25 ft
Note: CL stands for centerline and TYP means typical, as in that exact section is typical of others in that area.

Answer: D
Q13. A grid survey plot with spot elevations at each grid node is shown (100'×100' cells, contour interval 10). Which of the four contour drawings (A–D) correctly represents the elevations?
IVtopo

  • A) A
  • B) D
  • C) B
  • D) C
Compare the answers looking for differences in the contour lines drawn to eliminate answer choices. Contour lines should be successive (eg. 260 after 250). Choice B has the 240 contour out of place. Choice C has the 230, 240, 250, and 270 contours out of place. Choice D has the 230, 240, and 260 contours out of place.

Q14. The centerline of a highway drops 17.83 ft over a course of 314.21 ft horizontally. The rate of change is
Vvc
  • A) −0.06%
  • B) −5.67%
  • C) 0.06%
  • D) 5.60%
Grade = −\(\dfrac{17.83}{314.21}\)= −5.67%.

Q15. Stadia setup: K=100.50, C=0. Backsight to A: stadia interval 7.2−6.9 (angle 6°31'40" is extraneous — sight is level). Foresight to C: stadia interval 4.7−3.3, vertical angle 39°. What is the horizontal distance A to C?
IIstadia

  • A) 115.13 ft
  • B) 88.51 ft
  • C) 145.28 ft
  • D) 141.75 ft
Distance from Point A to instrument: \(D=K(s)+C\) D = 100.50(7.2−6.9)2 + 0 = 60.30' Distance from instrument to Point C: \(H=KI(\cos^2\alpha)\) H = 100.50(4.7−3.3)(cos39°)² = 84.98' Distance from Point A to Point C: AC = 60.30+84.98 = 145.28 ft
Note: The arrow of where the level is pointing is flat, therefore we don't take into account the 6° angle, which is extra information.

Answer: C
Q16. Lot corners: A (N3476.56, E1535.82), B (N−1617.16, E2127.39), C (N−2564.83, E−2131.91). What is the area of the parcel?
IIItravProgram A — partial
  • A) 315 acres
  • B) 255 acres
  • C) 212 acres
  • D) 198 acres
Shoelace formula: Area = \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left|X_A(Y_B-Y_C)+X_B(Y_C-Y_A)+X_C(Y_A-Y_B)\right|\)= 11,128,147.37 ft² = 255 acres

Answer: B
Q17. Triangle Building/Store/2+25 baseline: Δ1=63°40', Δ2=20°18', baseline segment (3+00 to 2+25) = 75 ft, (3+95 to 3+00) = 95 ft. What is the length from the SE corner of Building to NE corner of Store?
IIItravProgram T — full

  • A) 86.15'
  • B) 85.25'
  • C) 156.91'
  • D) 85'
Solve the small triangle (ASA): ∠A = 116.333°, ∠C = 43.3667° → law of sines gives b = 37.8935' Solve the larger triangle (law of cosines, sides 95, 37.8935, included angle 63.666°): x = 85.25'

Answer: B

Q18. An easement area needs recording. Line AB is 300 ft with a slope of 1/1.5 with respect to bearings N88°E/S2°E; what is the area of the 40-ft wide easement?
IIIarea

  • A) 0.245 ac
  • B) 0.265 ac
  • C) 0.235 ac
  • D) 0.255 ac
∠A = 90−tan⁻¹(\(\dfrac{1}{1.5}\)) = 56.31° X₁: x₁=\(\dfrac{40}{tan56.31}\)=26.67 ∠B=180−90−56.31=33.69° X₂: x₂=\(\dfrac{40}{tan33.69}\)=60 CD=300−26.67−60=213.33 trapezoid area = (\(\dfrac{40}{43560}\))[\(\dfrac{(300+213.33)}{2}\)] = 0.235 ac.
Note: When slope is in a fraction form, it is typically rise over run. So in this case it would be Y/X on the horizontal plane. However if it were in 1.5:1 form then it would be h:v or in this case x:y. Typically this form would be reserved for elevations rather than slope on an xy plane.

Answer: C
Q19. Distance measurements are to be taken in the Sierra National Forest. Which instrument would be used in a wooded area?
IIfield
  • A) Theodolite
  • B) EDM
  • C) Level
  • D) GPS
Tree canopy blocks GPS satellite connection theodolites/levels don't measure distance directly. An EDM is the only workable choice, though EDMs are typically inaccurate under 200 ft.

Answer: B
Q20. A high voltage power line will be extended through the foothills into the adjacent city. What type of survey is best used for this extension?
Iintro
  • A) Utility survey
  • B) Aerial survey
  • C) Route survey
  • D) Construction survey
For long stretches of linear works, a route survey is best utility survey only shows what exists, aerial isn't suited for long linear projects, construction survey is for build measurements.

Answer: C

IVtopo

B sits inside the 90 contour with no higher contour shown, so its elevation is anything between 90 and the next interval (100), but not exactly on a contour line — 98 is the best answer among the choices.

IIfield

A total station gives the most accurate coordinates at this range GPS is second-best.

Q24. The town wants to know if a new hotel is being built in an area marked on the FEMA Flood Map. Which survey does the city engineer need for the assessment?
Iintro
  • A) Topographic Survey

Q25. A circular borrow area has boundary elevation 1715' throughout; square-yard cross-section areas are given at +5/+10/+15/+20 ft above that boundary (65.5, 178.2, 93, 140 SY respectively). How much cut is there below elevation 1730 to level the borrow pit?
IIIarea

  • A) 210 yd³
  • B) 1870 yd³
  • C) 210 yd³
  • D) 1170 yd³
The elevation of the boundary of the borrow area is all 1715'. Therefore the cut below 1730' will be the difference between the two: 1730' − 1715' = 15' Everything at 15' and below is included in the cut: 5(65.5×9) + 10(178.2×9) + 15(93×9) + 15(140×9) = 50,440.5 ft³ \(\dfrac{50{,}440.5\text{ ft}^3}{27\text{ ft}}\times 1\text{ yd}^3\)= 1868.17 yd³ ≈ 1870 yd³
Video solution: exam1_q25_video_solution.mp4

Answer: B
Q26. Which of the following can be used to determine a watershed area?
IVtopo
  • A) Flood map

  • C) Parcel map
  • D) Topographic map
Watershed determination needs elevations/contours — a topographic map. Hydrological maps show water bodies, flood maps show flood risk, parcel maps are irrelevant here.

Q27. Paper size for a set of plans is standard 2'×3'. Scale is 1:180, with a 2-in margin on all sides. What is the maximum plotted area?
IVphoto
  • A) 3.31 ac

24"×36" sheet minus 2 in margins each side = 20"×32" = 640 in² at 1"=15 ft (180 in ÷ 12 in/ft), 1 in²=225 ft² 640 in² = 144,000 ft² = 3.31 ac.

Itheory

Approximate shift in vertical datum (in millimeters). Values shown are NAVD 88 minus NGVD 29. The Los Angeles area shows about 1000 mm: 1000 mm × \(\dfrac{1\text{ ft}}{304\text{ mm}}\)= 3.29 ft ≈ 3 ft

Q31. A severe storm knocked over a portion of a wooden property line fence adjacent to the neighbor. What should the homeowner do?
Ipls
  • A) None
  • B) Contact the City regarding the property line
  • C) Fix the fence with no outside contact
  • D) Hire a Land Surveyor
Since the property line is already established, the homeowner can replace the fence in kind (same location) without contacting anyone. A surveyor or the city only becomes necessary if a boundary dispute arises afterward.

Q32. Differential leveling field notes (BM R through BM S) have several blanks. The missing data for point C (a side-shot monument, FS=7.04, under the HI=125.69 set at TP2) is
IIlevel

  • A) 123.82 ft
  • B) 118.42 ft
  • C) 118.65 ft
  • D) 125.46 ft
Add BS, HI equals BS plus previous elevation, Subtract FS: 125.69 − 7.04 = 118.65
Note: When you see foresights underneath each other, you can assume that some of them are side shots (SS). Sometimes they will give you a SS column in the field notes too.

Answer: C
Q33. Which of the following applications can GIS be used for?
IVgis
  • A) Quantity takeoffs
  • B) Utility map
  • C) Mass diagram
  • D) Grading plans
A utility map which shows the locations of utilities is the best use for GIS of the answer choices. GIS in this case can quickly be used to determine of specific utilities lines run in a particular area. GIS is not as useful for grading plans as these plans are more detailed elevation rather than general contours. This would be too detailed for GIS use. The same goes for mass diagram and quantity takeoffs which basically calculate the amount of material needed for the project.

Answer: B
Q34. Two right triangles share vertical side X; left triangle has base 349.93' and base angle 33°0'0", right triangle (area 69,408 ft²) has base angle 39°0'0". What is distance X?
IIItheoryProgram T — partial

  • A) 414.04'
  • B) 142.14'
  • C) 124.82'
  • D) 136.79'
Adjacent side on longer triangle: \(\tan 33°=\dfrac{349.93}{\text{adjacent}}\) \(\text{adjacent}=\dfrac{349.93}{\tan 33°}\)= 538.85 Find X using triangle area formula and law of sine: \(\dfrac{(538.85-x)(y)}{2}\)= 69408 (538.85−x)(y) = 138816 \(\dfrac{\sin 51°}{538.85-x}=\dfrac{\sin 39°}{y}\) sin51°(y) = sin39°(538.85−x) \(y=\dfrac{\sin 39°(538.85-x)}{\sin 51°}\) \(y=\dfrac{339.109-0.6293x}{\sin 51°}\)= 436.348−0.80978x Substitute y in law of sine equation: (538.85−x)(436.348−0.80978x) = 138816 x = 124.82 or x = 952.88 X cannot be longer than 538.84 so it must be 124.82 x = 124.82'
Note: A problem like this is one of the main reasons that a TI-89 is useful. Since calculations are saved in the memory automatically, they can be recalled easily. When setting the two equations equal to solve for x, the solve function in the TI-89 can do this quickly - press F2 --> option 1 for solve(. For this solution you would enter solve((538.85-x)(436.35-0.80978x)=138816,x). You should see x=124.82 and x=952.88 as the answers. If you do not use a TI-89, you need to use the quadratic formula to find the x values. Of course x cannot be longer than 538.85 so 952.88 is invalid.
Student/instructor discussion: A student (J.B.) suggested a faster approach after finding 538.85: set up two equations for the area triangle directly — its area equals both ½·b·h and, using tan(39°)=b/h, this yields 538.85−414.03 = 124.815, matching the answer without the quadratic. The instructor confirmed this is also a valid way to solve it.

Answer: C
Q35. Point X (N550, E450), Point Y (N600, E875). Bearing of XZ = N28°47'E, bearing of YZ = N61°58'W. What are the coordinates of Point Z?
IIItravProgram H — full

  • A) N763.77, E567.42
  • B) N734.13, E536.81
  • C) N744.42, E547.24
  • D) N754.33, E556.85
Find Angle Z using the given bearings with Z as the common point. Find Angle X: \(\text{Angle }Z=S28°47'W+S61°58'E\)= 90.75° \(\text{Bearing }XY=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{875-450}{600-550}\right)\)= N83.29°E Angle X = 83.29° − 28°47' = 54.51° Find Northing/Easting of point Z using Law of Sine and components of Line XY: \(\text{Distance }XY=\sqrt{(600-550)^2+(875-450)^2}\)= 427.93ft \(\dfrac{\sin 90.75}{427.93}=\dfrac{\sin 54.51}{YZ}\rightarrow YZ\)= 348.46ft \(\text{Easting of }Z=875-348.46\sin(61°58')\)= E567.42ft \(\text{Northing of }Z=600+348.46\cos(61°58')\)= N763.77ft
Alternative Solution: You can also try trial and error and use each answer to see which matches the given XZ bearing. This can also be done using the YZ bearing. For example: \(\text{Bearing }XZ=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{567.42-450}{763.77-550}\right)\)= N28°46'E Keep trying until you find an answer that is the closest.

Answer: A
Q36. A highway profile has slope −0.79% starting at sta 1+80, 1.23% starting at sta 4+55, 3.43% starting at sta 9+20. Elevation at sta 0+20 is 177.47 ft. Assuming uniform slopes apply from each listed station forward, what is the elevation at sta 9+20?
Vvc
  • A) 193.82 ft
  • B) 195.54 ft
  • C) 198.07 ft
  • D) 208.34 ft
0+20→1+80 (160 ft @ −0.79%): −1.264 ft → elev 176.206 1+80→4+55 (275 ft @ 1.23%): +3.3825 → elev 179.588 4+55→9+20 (465 ft @ 3.43%): +15.9495 → elev 195.54 ft

Answer: B
Q37. Plane surveying is defined as
Itheory
  • A) surveying when less accurate surveying equipment is used
  • B) surveying when curvature of earth is considered
  • C) surveying when curvature of earth is neglected
  • D) surveying when refraction is only considered
Plane surveying treats the earth's surface as flat, neglecting curvature.

Answer: C
Q38. A rectangular park is proposed: 740±0.14 ft by 290±0.06 ft. What is the area of the park?
IIItheory
  • A) 214,600±0.20 ft²
  • B) 214,600±60.16 ft²
  • C) 214,600±85 ft²
  • D) 214,600±170 ft²
Error propagation: Error = √[(740²)(0.06²)+(290²)(0.14²)] = ±60.16 ft² Area = 740×290 = 214,600±60.16 ft².

Answer: B
Q39. A building pad has finished grade at 96 ft: 12 in concrete on 6 in aggregate base. Site plan: 150'×100' pad, corner elevations 98.5/98.5/96.0/96.0. What is the total excavation?
Varea

  • A) 1530 CY
  • B) 830 CY
  • C) 1560 CY
  • D) 2220 CY
Volume above finish grade elevation of 96 feet (average end area method times the area of pad): Volume = \(\dfrac{150\times 100\times(98.5-96)}{2}\)= 18750 ft³ Volume from 96 feet to the bottom of the aggregate base: Volume = \(\dfrac{12+6}{12}\times 100\times 150\)= 22500 ft³ Total volume = \((18750+22500)\dfrac{1\text{cy}}{27\text{ft}^3}\)= 1528 CY ≈ 1530 CY
Note: FG or finish grade means the final elevation at the top of the pad.

Answer: A
Q40. A mountain road in the Angeles Forest has 245 ft of proposed roadway length on this stretch (sheet 2). Given the contour map and the road cross-section (40% slope face, CP-to-HP at 0.75:1), what is the excavated volume for this stretch?
Varea

  • A) 73,000 CY
  • B) 22,000 CY
  • C) 37,000 CY
  • D) 51,000 CY
Elevation at the catch points A and B are 20' and 100', respectively. Use this change in elevation and the slope provided to determine the length of AB: \(\dfrac{100-20}{0.4}\)= 200 ft Find the area of the cross section triangle by first finding the length from A to the hinge point: A to HP = 200 − (80×0.75) = 140 ft Area of the triangle = \(\dfrac{1}{2}BH\) Area of the triangle = \(\dfrac{1}{2}(140)(80)\)= 5600 ft² Given the distance between contours and the fact that the slope line of the section are uniform, we can assume that the beginning and end of the roadway length will have the same cross section. Using the average end area method, both areas should be the same: V = \((L)\dfrac{A_1+A_2}{2}\) V = \((245)\dfrac{5600+5600}{2}\)= 1,372,000 ft³ = 50,814 CY ≈ 51,000 CY

Answer: D
Q41. A curve is staked from Point T (sta 12+45) to Point U. The straight (chord) distance T to U is 570 ft, central angle 35°. What is the approximate station at Point U?
VhcProgram S — full
  • A) 18+15
  • B) 5+79
  • C) 18+24
  • D) 15+24
C=2R·sin(\(\dfrac{Δ}{2}\)) → R=947.77' L=\(\dfrac{2πRΔ}{360}\)=578.96' station U = 12+45+578.96 = 18+23.96 ≈ 18+24

Answer: C
Q42. Backsight and foresight distances should be equal so that
IIlevel
  • A) Negate random user errors
  • B) Negate rod rounding errors
  • C) Minimize refraction and earth curvature errors
  • D) Keep the math easy
Balancing BS/FS distances cancels the effects of refraction and earth curvature, which act equally (in the same direction) on both sights when distances match.

Answer: C
Q43. A declining curve on a mass diagram indicates
Varea
  • A) excavation
  • B) lower elevation
  • C) cut
  • D) embankment
A falling mass diagram curve indicates material is being used as fill (embankment) — not necessarily a lower ground elevation, since the diagram tracks cumulative earthwork volume, not terrain elevation.

Answer: D
Q44. In a closed traverse, departures failed to close by −0.79' and latitudes by +0.49'. Horizontal traverse distance is 5649.2'. What is the approximate accuracy of the measurement?
IIItravProgram A — partial
  • A) 1/18850
  • B) 1/7150
  • C) 1/6100
  • D) 1/11550
This is the same as saying find the relative precision except we put it in ratio form where the top number in our ratio is 1. Find the length of the error to find the accuracy of measurement: \(\sqrt{(-0.79)^2+(0.49)^2}\)= 0.93 ft \(\dfrac{5649.2}{0.93}=\dfrac{6074}{1}\) 1 foot of error per 6074 feet length: accuracy ≈ \(\dfrac{1}{6100}\)

Answer: C
Q45. Starting at sta 7+47 the roadway will be repaved to a 2.1% slope. Existing centerline elevations are given via level notes (HI=465.80, FS 7.31 at 7+47, FS 8.14 at 8+23). What is the cut/fill at centerline 8+23?
Vvc

  • A) 0.77 fill
  • B) 0.77 cut
  • C) 2.43 fill
  • D) 2.43 cut
Elev existing 7+47 = 465.80−7.31=458.49 proposed elev at 8+23 = 458.49+(823−747)(0.021)=460.09 existing elev at 8+23 = 465.80−8.14=457.66 difference = 460.09−457.66 = 2.43 fill.

Answer: C
Q46. A contour map is requested for a 0.8×1.8 mile rectangular area, drawn on 24"×36" plans (margins ignored). Which scale is appropriate?
IVphoto
  • A) 1"=300'
  • B) 1"=250'
  • C) 1"=200'
  • D) 1"=650'
0.8 mi/24 in: \(\dfrac{0.8 mi}{24 in}\)=\(\dfrac{176 ft}{in}\) 1.8 mi/36 in: \(\dfrac{1.8 mi}{36 in}\)=\(\dfrac{264 ft}{in}\) pick the larger (more conservative) requirement so both directions fit → 1"=300'.

Answer: A
Q47. A development company owns a square 1.5-acre lot; the outer 5 ft is sidewalk/parkway. The rest is a multiuse building with underground parking, requiring excavation 15 ft deep with a 2:1 cut slope on each side. What is the total volume of cut?
Varea
  • A) 32,000 CY
  • B) 26,000 CY
  • C) 29,400 CY
  • D) 28,450 CY
\(1.5\text{ acres}=43560\times 1.5\)= 65340 ft² Length of each side of lot: \(\sqrt{65340}\)= 255.62' Parking lot dimensions: 255.62−5'−5' = 245.62' by 245.62' Volume of truncated square pyramid: \(V=\dfrac{1}{3}(a^2+ab+b^2)H\) a = 245.62 b = 245.62−2(15×2) = 185.62 \(V=\dfrac{1}{3}(245.62^2+185.62(245.62)+185.62^2)15\) V = 701879 ft³ = 25996 CY ≈ 26,000 CY

Answer: B
Q48. The chord AB of a circular curve is 327' and I=103°59'. What is the radius of arc AB?
VhcProgram S — full

  • A) 365.39 ft

  • C) 291.81 ft
  • D) 207.51 ft
C=2R·sin(\(\dfrac{Δ}{2}\)) → R =\(\dfrac{327}{(2·sin(51.9917^{\circ}))}\)= 207.51 ft

Answer: D
Q49. Using information from the slope stake, if Point E is at sta 1+35 with an elevation of 2115.32, the uniform grade between the center line of Point D and the centerline of Point E is
Vvc

  • A) 1.00%
  • B) 1.30%
  • C) 1.20%
  • D) 1.40%
Elevation at D_CL = 2136.03 + 1.17 − 1.7 + 0.9 Elevation at D_CL = 2136.4 ft Grade between the centerlines of D and E: \(\dfrac{2136.40-2115.32}{1757-135}\times 100\)= 1.3%

Answer: B
Q50. Which of the following has the highest accuracy for a horizontal control network?
Igis
  • A) Local control
  • B) Terrestrial-based control
  • C) Secondary control
  • D) Global-regional geodynamics
From highest order (most accurate) to lowest order (least accurate) horizontal control network: Global-regional geodynamics consist of GNSS-surveyed points that meet the Order AA accuracy requirements. These are primarily used for international deformation studies. Primary control consists of GNSS-surveyed points that meet the Order A accuracy requirements. These points are used for regional-local geodynamic and deformation studies. Secondary control densifies the network within areas surrounded by primary control, especially in high-value land areas and for high-precision engineering surveys. Secondary control surveys are executed to GNSS Order B standards. Terrestrial-based control is used for dependent control surveys to meet mapping, land information systems, property survey, and engineering needs. This network consists principally of stations set by traverse and triangulation to first- and second-order standards, and stations set using GNSS surveys to Order C standards. Local control provides reference points for local construction projects and small-scale topographic mapping. These surveys are referenced to higher-order control monuments and, depending on accuracy requirements, may be third-order class I, or third-order class II.

Answer: D
Q51. A roadway is converted to include a Class III bike lane; sign placed at edge of roadway at Point B. Horizontal curve radius to centerline 634' (minus 25' to arc ACD = 609'), Δ=70°, split 31°/39° at Point C. Vertical profile: PVI 57+23 elev 125.64, G1=3.5%, G2=−1.8%. F-F section: 50' wide, 2% cross-slope, B at edge. What is the elevation at Point B?
VvcProgram P — partial

  • A) 121.01 ft
  • B) 122.01 ft
  • C) 112.62 ft
  • D) 118.95 ft
Radius of Arc ACD: 634' − 25' = 609' Length of Arc ACD: \(L_{ACD}=\dfrac{2\pi RI}{360}=\dfrac{2\pi(609)(70)}{360}\)= 744.03' Length of Arc AC: \(L_{AC}=\dfrac{2\pi RI}{360}=\dfrac{2\pi(609)(70-31)}{360}\)= 414.53' Elevation at BVC (Note: Remember that the length of arc ACD is the same on the vertical curve as it is on the horizontal curve.): \(\text{elev}_{BVC}=\text{elev}_{PVI}-G\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)\) \(\text{elev}_{BVC}=125.64-3.5\left(\dfrac{7.4403}{2}\right)\)= 112.62' Elevation at Point C: \(\text{elev}_C=\dfrac{Rx^2}{2}+Gx+\text{elev}_{BVC}\) \(R=\dfrac{G'-G}{L}=\dfrac{-1.8-3.5}{7.4403}\)= −0.7123 \(\text{elev}_C=\dfrac{(-0.7123)(4.1453)^2}{2}+3.5(4.1453)+112.62\) elev C = 121.01 ft Elevation at Point B: elev B = 121.01 + 0.02(50) elev B = 122.01 ft

Q52. A vertical curve: BVC elev 567.92, G1=+1.78%, G2=−4.10%, L=750', EVC at sta 16+32. What is the station and elevation of the high point of the curve?
VvcProgram P — full

  • A) sta 6+55, elev 565.90
  • B) sta 11+67, elev 570.23
  • C) sta 11+09, elev 569.94
  • D) sta 6+55, elev 569.94
sta BVC = 16+32 − 7+50 sta BVC = 8+82 \(D_o=\dfrac{LG}{G-G'}\) \(D_o=\dfrac{7.5(1.78)}{1.78-(-4.1)}\) high point = 2+27 stations from BVC station of high point = 8.82 + 2.27 = 11+09 \(\text{elev}_{high\ point}=\dfrac{Rx^2}{2}+g_1x+\text{elev}_{BVC}\) \(R=\dfrac{g_2-g_1}{L}=\dfrac{-4.1-1.78}{7.5}\)= −0.784 \(\text{elev}_{high\ point}=\dfrac{-0.784(2.27)^2}{2}+1.78(2.27)+567.92\) elev high point = 569.94 ft
Only solve as far as you need to get a unique answer!

Q53. In an engineering project, what is the correct sequence used in developing a project from beginning to end?
Iintro
  • A) As-built, Construction Staking, Control, Topography
  • B) Construction Staking, Topography, Control, As-built
  • C) Control, Topography, Construction Staking, As-built
  • D) Topography, Control, As-built, Construction Staking
Control survey establishes basepoints → topographic survey maps existing conditions → construction staking marks locations for the engineering work → as-built survey records final elevations once complete.

Answer: C
Q54. BM #755 on Hartford Street has BS=7.1 ft, elevation 109.2 ft. Cross-sectional leveling at sta 3+78 on Jameson Drive gives the following FS/offset readings (right side):
5.76.41.93.14.95.33.3
362513071020
What is the elevation 17 ft right of centerline?
IIlevel
  • A) 112.4 ft
  • B) 109.3
  • C) 107.1
  • D) 112.9 ft
The given information in the table is the FS along the centerline at sta 3+78. We need to interpolate the elevation between the given information which is 10 feet right of the centerline and 20 feet right of the centerline. The assumption is that the FS changes linearly between those two points. Change in FS per foot from 10 feet right to 20 feet right of centerline: \(\dfrac{5.3-3.3}{10-20}\)= −0.2 FS feet per length from 10 feet right along centerline FS at 17 feet right of centerline = −0.2 × (17−10) + 5.3 = 3.9 FS Elevation at 17 feet right of centerline = 109.2 + 7.1 − 3.9 = 112.4 ft

Answer: A
Q55. The Terrace View Apartment building will be ten equally sized floors. The first three floors are built; the FS rod was located at the face of the building. Given BM1=122.50, BS=4.10, FS=8.75, H=61.20 ft, vertical angle 24° to the top of the third floor, what will the final elevation be at the top of the finished tenth floor?
IIstadia

  • A) 153.85 ft
  • B) 201.15 ft
  • C) 237.85 ft
  • D) 129.85 ft
Elevation of the Base (Ground level at the building): \(\text{Elev}_{\text{Base}}=BM1+BS-FS\) Elev Base = 122.50 ft + 4.10 ft − 8.75 ft Elev Base = 117.85 ft Considering that all the floors are equally sized, we can find the height of the 3rd floor, then divide by 3 to find the height of each floor, then multiple by 10 for the height of the tenth floor. Height of third floor: \(\text{Height}_{3rdFloor}=FS+H\tan(24°)\) Height  3rd Floor = 8.75 ft + 61.20 ft × tan(24°) Height  3rd Floor = 36.00 ft Height of tenth floor: \(\text{Height}_{EachFloor}=\dfrac{36}{3}\)= 12 feet Height  10th Floor = 12 feet × 10 floors = 120 feet Elevation of tenth floor: \(\text{Elev}_{10thFloor}=\text{Elev}_{Base}+\text{Height}_{10thFloor}\) Elev  10th Floor = 117.85 ft + 120 ft = 237.85 ft

Answer: C
